Welcome back! Claude shipped a feature that works while you sleep and something users weren’t told about, NVIDIA built a reconstruction system that audits itself, and Satya Nadella wants an emergency brake on every model.  In today's Atlas Newsletter: title: text Claude is running things you can’t see: One release Anthropic announced, and one users found by testing what Opus 5.5 shouldn’t know. NVIDIA researchers introduced GATOR: Casual photos in, simulation-ready 3D assets out, with an agent that edits its own meshes in Blender. A Claude skill that explains ideas by building them: Ask about a cache key and it invents a pin-tumbler lock you can take apart. Microsoft’s CEO says treat AI like a risky employee: Nadella’s rule: assume a model is compromised, then design around it. PS: Want to collaborate with the biggest GTM engine and distribution moat for AI companies? You can feature your tool with us and reach millions. Claude is running things you can't see Two things happened to Claude this week. One Anthropic announced. Every Pro and Max user on the waitlist now has Claude Code Projects.  You give Claude one ongoing goal and it splits the work into separate tasks, each running on its own in the background.  They keep going after you close your laptop, and you can check in from your phone. Each task can open code changes on GitHub and fix them when tests fail.  It carries memory across tasks, and it handles non-code work too, like reading a pile of support tickets for the most common problems.  It also burns through usage limits faster than regular Claude Code. The other thing, Anthropic hasn't said a word about. Users are convinced Opus 5.5 is being answered by a newer model. The test going around asks it about a recent benchmark it shouldn't know without searching. If it knows, people say you got the new one. TestingCatalog found a hidden item codenamed Arborio that looks like a Claude Health page for the web, a feature currently mobile-only in the US. Another, codenamed Iggy, shows nothing but a sun icon.  One guest at a New York AI dinner reported the room's consensus: Fable 5.5 will be stunning, and OpenAI will beat it in December with a model called Bel. Handing specific tasks to AI models will often make sense: they are much better than humans at many things. But AI's range of capabilities, allied to a convenient conversational interface and a seductively confident persona, raises the prospect less of delegation than of wholesale capitulation. Earlier this year I wrote a column about the risks of cognitive surrender to AI. Anxiety has only grown since.  My weekly newsletter for subscribers reveals the tiny workplace triumphs that recipients are proudest of. You can sign up here.  Andrew Palmer, Bartleby columnist Editor’s pick AI and the danger of cognitive surrender  How much should managers let bots do the thinking? Calculators didn’t make everyone innumerate. GPS navigation systems made driving easier. In any conversation about the cognitive effects of artificial intelligence, these two earlier technologies are reasonably likely to come up. Each is a useful entry-point into two big questions. How might AI change the way people think, and should managers do anything in response? From the Boss Class vault Presentations: It’s all in the knees How to captivate a room full of people To many workers the idea of presenting to a room of colleagues is nightmarish. Stumbling, umming and rambling is hard for the listener and nerve-racking for the speaker. Michael Chad Hoeppner is an actor-turned-presentation coach. On our “Boss Class” podcast the author of “Don’t Say Um” explains how an unusual technique might help presenters stay cool. Elsewhere in The Economist ▸ A no-rules approach to AI is mad politics and worse policy  ▸ The rise of the AI marketplace  ▸ Indian manufacturing’s moment may finally have arrived  Enjoying this newsletter? If you’re a subscriber you can get it in your inbox every Monday by signing up here. You’ll get more on work and office life from our management columnist.

🧠 Crypto News Brief: Bitcoin steadies above $84K as oil eases, but ETF outflows, a hardware-wallet supply-chain scare and Wednesday's CPI print keep traders cautious. In Washington, crypto rules now run through agencies and courts, not Congress. 📈 Bitcoin Holds Above $84,000 Despite $600M+ ETF Outflows Bitcoin is holding on to its weekend gains above $84,000 as oil prices slide, even though U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs bled more than $600 million in outflows last week. Altcoins are leading the bounce, with ether and solana each up more than 2% on the day. Read full story 🕵️ Ledger Confirms Unauthorized Implant in CryptoBilis-Sold Device Ledger says an unauthorized implant was found in at least one hardware wallet sold by CryptoBilis, its authorized reseller for Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines. Sales were paused on Oct. 9 after on-chain investigators estimated around $86M in user losses; Ledger urges recent CryptoBilis buyers not to set up their devices and to move funds to a new device with a fresh seed, while stressing its own systems were not compromised. More details 🐞 Inside the Hidden XRP Ledger Bug That Threatened the 100B Supply Cap A new deep dive examines how a decade-old XRP Ledger flaw, which could have created billions of dollars' worth of XRP from nothing, went undetected for years before being patched. The episode reopens questions about auditing legacy code in long-running blockchains. Read more ⚖️ Prediction Markets Edge Toward a Supreme Court Showdown States and platforms alike now want the U.S. Supreme Court to decide whether sports event contracts are state-regulated gambling or CFTC-regulated swaps. The push comes days after the CFTC moved to fold event contracts into its swaps rules as the legal fight intensifies. See details 🏛️ CLARITY Act's Collapse Hands the Crypto Rulebook to Regulators With the market-structure bill dead after a 49–50 Senate cloture vote, U.S. crypto policy now rests on SEC and CFTC rulemaking. Analysis suggests that path could speed innovation while favoring incumbents; comments on the SEC's proposed Regulation Crypto Assets close October 20.
